name: Mali
tagline: Timbuktu, Djenne, and the Niger bend
summary: The mud-brick mosque at Djenne is the largest building of its kind on earth, the Bandiagara escarpment holds Dogon villages built into the cliff, and the Niger loops nine hundred kilometres north into the desert before turning back.
when: November to February, after the rains and before the heat. Check advice: the north and centre are not currently travelled.

entries.caption: The Great Mosque of Djenne
entries.description: The largest mud-brick building in the world, re-plastered by the whole town every spring.
entries.subject: the mud-brick Great Mosque of Djenne with its wooden toron beams

entries.caption: The Niger Bend
entries.description: The river runs north into the Sahara, thinks better of it, and turns southeast.
entries.subject: the Niger river curving broad and brown through Sahelian scrub

entries.caption: Elephants in the Gourma
entries.description: The Gourma herd makes the longest elephant migration in Africa, on a loop into Burkina Faso.
entries.subject: desert-adapted elephants crossing dry Sahelian scrub in the Gourma

entries.caption: Not the Business Here
entries.description: There is no lodge circuit. The Gourma elephants are a conservation story, not a game drive.
entries.subject: acacia and dry grassland in the Gourma with a waterhole

entries.caption: The Bandiagara Escarpment
entries.description: A hundred and fifty kilometres of sandstone cliff, with villages built into the face of it.
entries.subject: Dogon villages built into the cliff face of the Bandiagara escarpment

entries.caption: Falls at Woroni
entries.description: Small falls on the sandstone plateau above Bandiagara, running only after the rains.
entries.subject: a seasonal waterfall over sandstone on the Dogon plateau

entries.caption: The Niger and Lake Debo
entries.description: Pinasses working the river between Mopti and Timbuktu, and the inland delta spreading behind them.
entries.subject: a loaded pinasse under sail on the Niger near Mopti

entries.caption: River Sand, Not Sea
entries.description: Landlocked — the beaches here are sandbars on the Niger, and people swim off them.
entries.subject: a sandbar and shallow water on the Niger river at low season

entries.caption: The Gallery Forest
entries.description: Ribbons of woodland along the river, and the baobabs standing alone on the plain behind.
entries.subject: a large baobab standing alone on Sahelian grassland

entries.caption: Walking the Dogon Country
entries.description: Village to village along the escarpment, sleeping on roofs, four days or fourteen.
entries.subject: walkers on a path below the Bandiagara cliff at first light

entries.caption: Where the Blues Came From
entries.description: Ali Farka Toure, Toumani Diabate, Salif Keita and Tinariwen are all from here.
entries.subject: a kora player performing at an evening gathering in Bamako

entries.caption: Dogon, Bambara, Tuareg, Fulani
entries.description: Dogon on the escarpment, Bambara on the river, Tuareg and Fulani on the plains north of it.
entries.subject: a Dogon elder outside a granary with a carved door

entries.caption: Tigadege Na and Capitaine
entries.description: Groundnut stew, and Nile perch grilled whole on the riverbank at Mopti.
entries.subject: grilled capitaine fish with rice and onion sauce on a plate

entries.caption: The Sigui and the Dama
entries.description: Dogon masked ceremonies, the Sigui every sixty years and the Dama for the dead.
entries.subject: Dogon dancers in tall kanaga masks in a village square

entries.caption: Bogolan and Bamana Sculpture
entries.description: Mud-dyed bogolanfini cloth, Bamana chiwara antelope crests, and Dogon carved doors.
entries.subject: a length of mud-dyed bogolan cloth in black and ochre

entries.caption: Timbuktu
entries.description: Three mud mosques, and a library tradition that ran to hundreds of thousands of manuscripts.
entries.subject: the mud-brick Sankore mosque in Timbuktu

entries.caption: Four Sites, All at Risk
entries.description: Djenne, Timbuktu, Bandiagara and the Tomb of Askia — every one of them on the danger list.
entries.subject: the stepped pyramid tomb of Askia at Gao

entries.caption: Bamako and Mopti
entries.description: A capital sprawling both sides of the Niger, and a port town built on three islands.
entries.subject: the Niger riverfront and pirogues at Mopti

entries.caption: Sudano-Sahelian
entries.description: Mud walls, projecting palm beams, and buttressed towers — a style that belongs to this river.
entries.subject: the buttressed mud facade and wooden beams of a Sahelian mosque

entries.caption: Monday Market at Djenne
entries.description: The whole delta comes to the square in front of the mosque, once a week.
entries.subject: the Monday market crowd in front of the Great Mosque of Djenne

entries.caption: Hard Country for It
entries.description: The security situation makes most of Mali unvisitable at present, and that is the honest answer.
entries.subject: children playing in a village square in southern Mali

entries.caption: The Escarpment on Foot
entries.description: The Dogon country is walking country, and always has been.
entries.subject: a narrow path climbing between rocks on the Bandiagara escarpment

entries.caption: Almost None
entries.description: A handful of hotels in Bamako. The rest of the country is guesthouses and roofs.
entries.subject: a courtyard hotel with mud walls in Bamako

entries.caption: Re-Plastering Djenne
entries.description: Every year the town rebuilds the mosque's surface by hand in a single day.
entries.subject: the whole town plastering the Great Mosque of Djenne by hand

entries.caption: Mud and Long Shadows
entries.description: Djenne an hour before sunset, when the toron beams throw stripes down the wall.
entries.subject: low sun on the mud wall and projecting beams of Djenne's mosque

entries.caption: The Tomb of Askia
entries.description: A pyramid of mud at Gao, built in 1495 for the emperor of Songhai.
entries.subject: the mud pyramid tomb of Askia at Gao with wooden beams

entries.caption: Why Mali
entries.description: Because Djenne, Timbuktu and the Dogon country are three of the great sights of Africa.
entries.subject: a lone figure in front of the Great Mosque of Djenne
